newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Relieved Russia hails own success in Belarus.
newsitem.headline: Relieved Russia hails own success in Belarus.

text.p: Russia, after flexing its diplomatic muscle to defuse an ugly political crisis across the border in Belarus, took credit for a successful compromise on Friday.
"This is a huge success, a genuine breakthrough in the search for a way out of the constitutional crisis in Belarus," Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky told a news briefing.

But the tension in Minsk, Moscow's closest ally among former Soviet states, is unlikely to disappear, leaving Russia treading a fine line between backing hardline pro-Moscow President Alexander Lukashenko and pushing him to accept economic reforms.
Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, whose all-night talks broke the deadlock between Lukashenko and the Minsk parliament, insisted he had not forced the deal through.
Yastrzhembsky also stressed Russia was not bullying its small but strategically important neighbour.

"For we Russians it was extremely important that the Russian side, respecting the sovereignty of a fraternal republic and without interfering in its internal affairs, played a role in the search for a political compromise," Yastrzhembsky said.
Analysts and diplomats said it was clear, however, that Chernomyrdin had put pressure on Lukashenko.
The president, who under threat of impeachment insisted he would share his rule with no one and dissolve parliament if necessary, is seeking sweeping new powers in a referendum.
On Friday, however, he accepted parliament's position that Sunday's plebiscite would not be legally binding and that a national congress be convened to debate a new constitution.

Russia, which formed a two-state economic community with Belarus in April, has been slower than some states to criticise the failure of Lukashenko, an avowed nostalgist for the Soviet Union, to undertake free market and democratic reforms.
But as the conflict grew this week with the prospect of instability on Russia's borders, Moscow's patience wore thin. Yeltsin and Chernomyrdin called urgently for compromise.

Deputy prime minister Valery Serov said after talks with Belarus legislators on Wednesday: "We have joined our destinies in the economy. It's time now to stop all these political battles and get down to concrete economic measures."
Arkady Moshes, an analyst at Moscow's Institute of Europe, said the economic pressure Russia can bring to bear on Belarus's population of 10 million may have been a key factor in the deal.

"Lukashenko has nowhere to turn. His prospects would be pretty short-lived if he antagonised Russia," he said. "As long as there is no economic reform in Belarus, he will be forced to depend on those subsidies he gets from time to time."
For Moscow, Lukashenko's attraction is his pursuit of closer ties with Russia -- something the Kremlin would like to see more of elsewhere in the former Soviet Union.
So despite disapproving of his economic disarray and repression of opponents, Russia sees the Belarus president as "a bird in the hand", Moshes said. He was better than the unknown.
However Viktor Kremenyuk, deputy head of the USA and Canada Institute think-tank, warned that Moscow may find it hard to keep Lukashenko obliging Russia's interests.
"I am not sure anyone has a chance of influencing Lukashenko," he said. "He is so unpredictable and ambitious."
Kremenyuk said fundamental divisions were likely to persist in Belarus, ensuring Moscow's headaches would continue.
But few observers see a likelihood of Russia being drawn into any sort of military conflict in Belarus.

Convalescence from heart surgery has limited Yeltsin's role in the Belarus talks, leaving Chernomyrdin to fly to Minsk and negotiate in a manner that recalled the premier's success in ending the Chechen hostage crisis at Budennovsk in July 1995.

But the Kremlin, always anxious to avoid being upstaged, was quick to underline the president's role in reaching a compromise. Yastrzhembsky stressed Yeltsin had talked to Lukashenko by telephone on Thursday and that it was he who had dispatched the prime minister to Minsk.
"The personal contribution of President Yeltsin in working out the Russian position and bringing the two opposing sides in Belarus closer together is indisputable," the spokesman said.
